Problem formalization. Following existing work (Wang et al., 2020), we formulate the dialogue process as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). At each turn $t$ , according to the observation on the current state $s_t$ , i.e. the dialogue history $\{u_1^{sys}, u_1^{usr}, \dots, u_t^{sys}, u_t^{usr}\}$ , the dialogue system se

lects an action $a_{t} \in \mathcal{A}$ , where $u^{sys}$ and $u^{usr}$ represent the system and user utterances, $\mathcal{A}$ is a set of candidate strategies pre-defined by domain experts. Then, guided by this action $a_{t}$ , the system player generates the utterance $u_{t+1}^{sys}$ . In return, the user player responds to the system with $u_{t+1}^{usr}$ . This process repeats until the dialogue goal is achieved or the maximum number of turns $T$ is reached. The objective is to learn a policy $\pi_{\theta}$ maximizing the expected cumulative rewards over observed dialogue episodes as:

$$
\pi^ {*} = \arg \max  _ {\pi_ {\theta}} \left[ \sum_ {t = 0} ^ {T} r \left(s _ {t}, a _ {t}\right) \right], \tag {1}
$$

where $r(\cdot)$ is a reward function, abbreviated as $r_t$ .

LLM-powered role simulation. Following previous work (Deng et al., 2023b), we employ two LLMs as a user and an assistant to simulate dynamic user-assistant interactions. Role descriptions, along with instructions about their corresponding conversational goals, are delivered to each LLM. Furthermore, we prompt an LLM, following PPDPP (Deng et al., 2023b), to act as a critic for evaluating the dialogue states. The prompts utilized for role simulation and state evaluation processes remain consistent with those employed in PPDPP. Please refer to Appendix G for detailed prompts. Through this approach, we can concentrate our research efforts on effectively planning strategies for each dialogue turn.

We aim to demonstrate the efficacy of this framework by primarily comparing against PPDPP. Additionally, we follow PPDPP to compare with a general fine-tuning dialogue model DialoGPT (Zhang et al., 2019), and a range of prompting-based methods, including Standard Prompting, Proactive (Deng et al., 2023a), ProCoT (Deng et al., 2023a), Ask-an-Expert (Zhang et al., 2023a), and ICL-AIF (Fu et al., 2023). Following Deng et al. (2023b), we report the results of baselines.

In line with PPDPP (Deng et al., 2023b), we instantiate the policy LM utilizing RoBERTa-large (Liu et al., 2019). We implement MCTS using codes from GDPZero (Yu et al., 2023). We also employ gpt-3.5-turbo-0613 as the static LLM for both the playing system and the user, alongside the reward model. All used prompts and temperatures are consistent with PPDPP. Additionally, we adhere to the same mapping $\mathcal{M}_a$ of natural language instructions with PPDPP for dialogue actions. For more training details, please refer to the Appendix C.

Due to the absence of complete trajectories in the training set of CIMA, only dialogue fragments are available. Therefore, we can not apply the same optimization method as on ESConv. In this section, we introduce the pretraining process on CIMA.

For the policy network, since actual state-action values cannot be obtained without complete trajectories, we utilize a Q-Network for approximation. The optimization loss is as follows:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {L} _ {p r e, \theta} = \sum_ {t = 1} ^ {T} \left[ \left(\hat {Q} _ {\beta} \left(s _ {t}, a _ {t}\right) - Q ^ {*} \left(s _ {t}, a _ {t}\right)\right) \right. \\ \left. \log \pi_ {\theta} \left(a _ {t} \mid s _ {t}\right) \right], \\ \end{array}
$$

$$
Q ^ {*} (s _ {t}, a _ {t}) = R (a _ {t} | s _ {t}) + \gamma * \max _ {a ^ {\prime}} Q _ {\beta} (s _ {t + 1}, a ^ {\prime}),
$$

where $\hat{Q}_{\beta}(s_t, a_t)$ means using the Q-network $Q_{\beta}$ to calculate state-action values with stopping gradient. $R(a_t|s_t)$ is the reward calculated by the same method as on ESConv but with different maps. We map "incorrect answer", "no answer", "partially correct answer" and "correct answer" as -1.0, -0.5, 0.5, and 1.0. Simultaneously, the optimization loss for Q-network is as follows:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {L} _ {p r e, \beta} = \sum_ {t = 1} ^ {T} \left[ Q ^ {*} \left(s _ {t}, a _ {t}\right) - Q _ {\beta} \left(s _ {t}, a _ {t}\right) \right] ^ {2}, \\ Q ^ {*} (s _ {t}, a _ {t}) = R (a _ {t} | s _ {t}) + \gamma * \max  _ {a ^ {\prime}} Q _ {\beta} (s _ {t + 1}, a ^ {\prime}). \\ \end{array}
$$

Finally, the overall loss for pretraining on CIMA is as follows:

$$
\mathcal {L} _ {p r e} = \mathcal {L} _ {p r e, \theta} + \lambda_ {1} * \mathcal {L} _ {p r e, \beta}. \tag {6}
$$

The training process for policy LM comprises two phases: offline RL-based pretraining (PT) and MCTS-guided self-play training (SPT). In the pretraining phase, DPDP is trained on the training set with collected rewards for each turn, and the checkpoint is saved based on the best performance observed on the validation set. Subsequently, during the MCTS-guided self-play training, cases from the training set are randomly sampled for online training. Due to cost considerations, we did not conduct an extensive hyperparameter search on ESConv. Table 7: Hyper-parameter settings in two-stage training phases for CraigslistBargain.
Training PhaseHyperparameterValue
PTBatch Size8
Training Epochs10
Learning Rate6e-6
Max Sequence Length512
Discount Factor0.999
Loss Weight λ11.0
SPTTraining Epochs3
Learning Rate1e-6
Max Conversation Turn5
Discount Factor0.999
Loss Weight λ21.0
Training Size per Epoch100
We mainly used the primary hyperparameters from PPDPP on ESConv and only conducted a search for learning rates within the range of [1e-6, 6e-6, 1e-5] on CIMA. The hyperparameters employed in our experiments are exhaustively detailed in Table 5, 6, and 7. All experiments are executed on a server equipped with 1 NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU. Pretraining needs 128/6/210 minutes and self-play training needs 5/3/15.5 hours for ESConv/CIMA/CraisglistBargain.
